The '''Brown–Gibson model''' is one of the many techniques for [[Multi-criteria decision analysis|multi-attribute decision making]]. The method was developed in 1972 by P. Brown and D. Gibson.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Phillip A. |last2=Gibson |first2=David F. |title=A Quantified Model for Facility Site Selection-Application to a Multiplant Location Problem |journal=AIIE Transactions |volume=4 |number=1 |pages=1–10 |year=1972 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |doi=10.1080/05695557208974822 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/05695557208974822|url-access=subscription }}
</ref> This is one of the few models which integrates both [[objectivity (science)|objective]] and [[subjectivity|subjective]] factors in [[decision making]].

The Brown–Gibson model can be [[mathematics|mathematically]] represented as follows:

: <math> M_i = C_i \cdot \big[ D \cdot O_i + (1 - D) S_i \big] </math>

where

''M''<sub>''i''</sub> = measure for an alternative ''i''

''C''<sub>''i''</sub> = critical [[design of experiments|factor]] measure, which could be either 0 or 1 for an alternative ''i''

''O'' = [[Objectivity (philosophy)|objective factor]] measure, which could be between 0 and 1; however, the sum of all objective factor measures for different alternatives should add back to 1

''S'' = [[Subject (philosophy)|subjective factor]] measure, which could be between 0 and 1; however, the sum of all subjective factor measures for different alternatives should add back to 1

''D'' = objective factor decision weight; should be between 0 and 1

One would select the alternative whose measure is the highest.
